message.content:
**Answer**

The most recent common ancestor of a lion (*Panthera leo*) and a zebra (*Equus quagga*) is the last common ancestor of the two orders that contain them: **Carnivora** (lions) and **Perissodactyla** (zebras).  
That ancestor is the last common ancestor of the entire clade **Laurasiatheria**, which includes all of those orders plus others such as Artiodactyla (even‑toed ungulates), Chiroptera (bats), Cetartiodactyla (whales, hippos, etc.), and Eulipotyphla (hedgehogs, moles, shrews).

**Timeframe**

- The divergence between Carnivora and Perissodactyla is estimated to have occurred roughly **90–100 million years ago** during the late Cretaceous period.  
- Thus, the last common ancestor of lions and zebras lived around that time, making it a member of the early Laurasiatherian radiation.

**Why this matters**

- This ancestor is far older than the last common ancestor of all mammals (≈200 million years ago) but younger than the last common ancestor of all vertebrates.  
- It represents the point at which the lineages that would become modern carnivores and odd‑toed ungulates split off from their shared ancestors.

So, in short: **the last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, dating back about 90–100 million years ago.**
